items.prose: A thread reads a 6 MiB file in 8 KiB reads. One system call costs 0.2 µs.
items.question: How many microseconds of call overhead does the whole read cost?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the calls first, then multiply by 0.2 µs.

byKey.calls: 768 is the number of calls. Multiply by 0.2 µs.

explain.text: 6 MiB is 6,291,456 bytes and 8 KiB is 8,192, so 768 calls. At 0.2 µs each that is 153.6 µs.

items.question: Which of these makes the kernel switch to another thread?

options.text: A `recv` on an empty socket, which blocks

options.why: A call that returns at once stays on the same thread: no switch.
That never enters the kernel at all.

options.text: A `read` of 8 bytes already in memory
options.why: The kernel copies the bytes and returns to the same thread.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which call puts its thread to sleep?

explain.text: A blocking receive on an empty socket sleeps the thread, so the kernel runs another one. The other calls return to the thread that made them.

items.prose: A stream of 24-byte frames is read in chunks of 60, 50 and 60 bytes: 170 bytes in all. Leftover bytes carry over to the next read.
items.question: Fill in the totals.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Carry the leftover into each new chunk.

byKey.r0c1: Reads parse 2, 2 and 3 frames: 60, then 12 + 50, then 14 + 60.

explain.text: $170 = 7 \times 24 + 2$. The reads parse 2, 2 and 3 frames, and 2 bytes wait for the next read.

items.prose: A reader loops on a TCP connection, and its `recv` returns 0.
items.question: What should the reader do?

options.text: Treat it as ended and close its side
Wait for data and call `recv` again
options.why: The 0 will come back at once, every time, so the loop would spin.

options.text: Report an error, since errors return 0
options.why: An error returns -1. Zero is an orderly close.

options.text: Parse a frame of zero bytes
options.why: A close carries no data, so there is no frame to parse.

feedback.correct: Treat it as the end of the stream.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does 0 mean on a TCP socket?

explain.text: On TCP, `recv` returns 0 only when the peer has closed. The reader should finish with what it has and close its own side.

items.prose: The round trip between a client and a server is 36 ms.
items.question: When does TCP's first data reach the server, in milliseconds?

widget.accept: 54 ms: three one-way trips of 18 ms. UDP needs 18 ms.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count three one-way trips of 18 ms.

byKey.udp: 18 ms is UDP's time. TCP waits for the handshake first.
byKey.rtt: The data needs a third trip after the SYN and the SYN-ACK.

explain.text: One way is 18 ms. SYN, SYN-ACK and then the data make three trips: 54 ms. UDP sends at once and arrives at 18 ms.

items.prose: Sequence numbers 2, 3, 6, 9, 4 and 8 arrive, in that order.
items.question: How many numbers from 1 up to the largest never arrived?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List 1 to 9 and cross off what arrived.

byKey.seen: 6 is how many arrived. Count the absent ones.

explain.text: The largest is 9. Numbers 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 9 arrived, so 1, 5 and 7 are missing.

items.prose: Four bytes in a big-endian field read `00 00 07 d0`.
items.question: What number do they hold?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first byte is the most significant.

byKey.le: You read the bytes little-endian. The wire is big-endian.

items.prose: A price of −100 pence goes on the wire as four big-endian bytes.
items.question: What is the last byte, as a decimal?

widget.accept: 156: $256 - 100$, which is 0x9c. The bytes are `ff ff ff 9c`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take 100 away from a multiple of 256.

byKey.mag: 100 is the last byte of +100. The negative value is its complement.

explain.text: −100 is $2^{32} - 100$, which ends in 256 − 100 = 156. The four bytes are `ff ff ff 9c`.

items.prose: A handler takes feeds A and B. Each loses 2% of 1,000,000 messages, independently.
items.question: On average, how many messages do both feeds lose?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Both copies must be lost together.

byKey.one: 20,000 is what one feed loses alone.
byKey.sum: You added the two losses. A message is gone only when both feeds drop it.

explain.text: A message is lost for good only if both copies are: $0.02 \times 0.02 = 0.0004$. Of 1,000,000 that is 400 on average.

items.prose: A wire frame packs its fields in this order with no padding: a 1-byte type, a 4-byte sequence number, an 8-byte order id, a 4-byte price and a 4-byte quantity. Offsets count from 0.
items.question: At which byte offset does the price start?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the sizes of the fields before the price.

byKey.aligned: That is the offset in a host struct with natural alignment. The wire frame has no padding.
byKey.from-one: You counted from 1. The first byte is offset 0.

explain.text: The type, sequence number and order id take $1 + 4 + 8 = 13$ bytes, so the price starts at offset 13. A host struct would pad it to 16, which is why the frame is written byte by byte.
